869.title: Flame from flame
869.hook: is the one reborn the same person? like a flame lit from another flame, neither the same nor different (Milinda, Book 2)
869.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often explain rebirth with Nagasena's lamp images from the Questions of King Milinda: a continuing of causes, neither the same person nor a different one, with no soul passing across.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chariot: no single part is the chariot, and the name gathers them all. Your line was a name for parts. Did you catch your own name gathering anything up? Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

If a name is only a name for parts, the king has a sharper question waiting. Buddhists speak of rebirth. So when a life ends and another begins, he asks, is the one who is born the same as the one who died, or someone else? It's a trap with two doors. Say the same, and there's a fixed self after all, carried from body to body. Say someone else, and why should anyone care what happens to that stranger? Nagasena takes neither door. Neither the same, he says, nor another. And then, as always, he reaches for something you could hold in your hand.
screen: `SAME PERSON, OR SOMEONE ELSE?` → `A TRAP WITH TWO DOORS.` → `NEITHER THE SAME, NOR ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, a lamp through the night. Nagasena asks: if a man lights a lamp and it burns all night, is the flame in the first watch of the night the same as the flame in the middle watch? No, says the king. And the last watch? Not the same either. Then were there several lamps? No, the king says, the light burned all night from the same lamp. Just so, says Nagasena: one moment arises as another passes, and the line runs on, neither the same nor another. Second, a lamp lit from a lamp. Elsewhere in the book the king asks whether rebirth happens without anything passing over. Yes, Nagasena says. When one lamp is lit from another, nothing moves across: no little piece of the first flame travels. Yet the second is lit, and it would not be burning without the first. Third, a verse from a teacher. The king has learned verses from his own teacher as a boy. Did the verse transmigrate from the teacher into him? No. Yet he has it, and he has it because of the teacher. Fourth, why the image matters. A flame lit from a flame is not a soul moving house, and it is not a stranger either. It is a cause and what it causes, close enough to be responsible for, open enough to change. That is the shape Nagasena gives to rebirth, and his night-long lamp shows it at work within one life too. On that picture, the person who started this lesson a few minutes ago is already a later flame of the same lamp. In the Theravada telling, what carries on is not a thing but a continuing: each flame owing its light to the one before.
screen: `ONE LAMP, BURNING ALL NIGHT.` · `A FLAME LIT, AND NOTHING PASSES OVER.` · `A VERSE LEARNED FROM A TEACHER.` · `NOT A SOUL MOVING HOUSE.` · then, large: `NEITHER THE SAME NOR ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one flame from another, if you can do it safely. Two candles, or a candle and a taper. Light the first, then tip the second to it and watch the new flame catch. If there's no candle nearby, bring the picture to mind instead. Then sit with the breath. Each breath arises from the one before, and none of them is the same breath. Watch one end and the next begin. The bell holds the time.
Flame from flame. Nagasena's picture of rebirth: nothing passes across from one flame to the next, yet the second burns because of the first. Today's word.
Your line: flame from flame. Today, notice one thing you do that you caught from someone else, a phrase, a habit, a kindness, and name who lit it. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

Nagasena uses that as a picture of rebirth with nothing passing over.

fork.setup: you're Nagasena. the king asks: is the one who is reborn the same person as the one who died, or someone else?
options: the same person, carried over.
someone else entirely.
neither the same nor another.
fork.reveal: he refuses both doors and reaches for a lamp: the flame at dusk and the flame at dawn are not the same, yet it is one lamp burning all night.

what it means: in Nagasena's telling, nothing passes across; a new flame burns because of the old one, neither the same nor another.

870.title: The stolen mango
870.hook: is the thief responsible for mangoes that grew from the one he took? yes (Milinda, Book 2)
870.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use Nagasena's mango and fire cases to explain kamma and rebirth together: no fixed self passes across, yet a life is not cut off from the deeds it grew from.

segments.voice: Yesterday, flame from flame: nothing passes across, yet the new flame burns because of the old. Your line was flame from flame. Who lit something in you? Today, the king pushes harder. Day eight hundred seventy.

Here's the loophole the king spots. If the one reborn is neither the same nor another, then maybe the new one gets off clean. A fresh flame, a fresh start. Why should anyone answer for what an earlier flame did? It sounds like a legal argument, and Nagasena answers it like one. He takes the king into a courtroom. A man is dragged before the king by a farmer, who says: this man stole my mangoes. And the thief has a clever defense ready.
screen: `A FRESH FLAME, A FRESH START?` → `A FARMER, A THIEF, A KING.` → `A CLEVER DEFENSE.`

segments.voice: First, the defense. Your majesty, the thief says, I never took the mangoes this man planted. He put a mango in the ground. The ones I picked grew on the tree that came up from it. Those are different mangoes. So I'm not guilty of taking his. Second, the verdict. Nagasena asks the king: would that man deserve punishment? Yes, says the king. Why? Because, whatever he says, the mangoes he took grew from the one the farmer planted. They are the farmer's because they came from his. Third, the turn. Just so, Nagasena says. A person does good or bad in this life, and from those deeds another name and form is born. So the deeds are not escaped. The new life grew from the old one the way the fruit grew from the planted mango. Nagasena gives the king more cases of the same shape. A man lights a fire in the cold season to warm himself and walks off without putting it out. It spreads and burns a neighbor's field. He says: the fire I lit is not the fire that burned your field. The king says he is responsible anyway, because one fire came from the other. Fourth, what this keeps together. Yesterday's flame said nothing fixed passes across. Today's mango says that doesn't make you a stranger to your own past. Both answers stand at once. In this passage, kamma isn't pictured as a judge handing out sentences from outside. It's fruit growing from what was planted. The mango doesn't need anyone to carry it from the seed. It grows from the seed anyway. And it grows on any ordinary day, not only across lives: the word said yesterday, the promise left lying, the fire not put out.
screen: `THESE AREN'T THE MANGOES HE PLANTED.` · `GUILTY: THEY GREW FROM HIS.` · `A FIRE LEFT BURNING, A FIELD LOST.` · `KAMMA: FRUIT FROM WHAT WAS PLANTED.` · then, large: `THE MANGO GREW FROM YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: own one consequence. Let the body settle into the seat. Bring to mind one small thing that happened because of something you did, kind or careless. A message you sent. A door you held, or didn't. Don't argue the case. Don't build a clever defense. Just let it be yours: this grew from that. Notice what it's like to hold it without excuse and without punishment. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The stolen mango. Nagasena's courtroom case: the thief is guilty, because the fruit he took grew from the one that was planted. Today's word.
Your line: the mango grew from yours. Today, when something comes back to you, good or hard, trace it to the seed you planted before reaching for a defense. Day eight hundred seventy.

options: not guilty. different mangoes.

fork.reveal: the king says guilty, and Nagasena springs the point: just so, a new life grows from the deeds of the old one.

original.note: Pali: mango. the fruit in Nagasena's courtroom case.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a thief and some fruit.
what it means: no self passes across, yet the new life isn't a stranger to the old: it grew from those deeds.
what a scholar hears: the same dialogue sets the mango beside other cases, like a fire left burning, all to hold not-self and kamma together.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, Book 2 (the mango thief and the fire left burning)

871.title: Milk to curd
871.hook: milk becomes curd, then butter: continuity without a fixed thing (Milinda, Book 2)
871.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use Nagasena's milk, curd, butter and ghee image to explain how a life continues without a fixed self: each state arises from the one before.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stolen mango: the thief is guilty, because the fruit grew from what was planted. Your line was the mango grew from yours. Did anything come back to you that you'd planted? Day eight hundred seventy-one.

A baby photo, propped on a shelf. Somebody lying on their back, tiny, not yet able to hold up their own head. Is that the grown person who walks past it every morning? The quick answer is yes. But that baby had no words, none of the grown person's memories, hands a fraction of the size. So in what sense is it the same one? Nagasena puts exactly this to the king, and the king's first answer is no: that baby was someone else. Nagasena shows him what that answer would cost, and then he reaches into a kitchen.
screen: `A PHOTO OF A BABY.` → `IS THAT YOU?` → `THE KING SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, the cost of saying no. If the baby and the grown king are simply two different people, Nagasena says, then the grown king would have had no mother, no father, no teacher at all. The boy who goes to school would be one person and the one who finishes his learning another. The one who does a wrong would be different from the one who answers for it. The king sees where this leads and asks what Nagasena would say instead. Second, Nagasena's answer. I was that tender baby, he says, and I am this grown man. They are held together as one by dependence on this same body, one moment depending on the one before. Third, the kitchen. Milk is taken from the cow. After a while it turns to curd. From curd, butter. From butter, ghee. Would it be right, Nagasena asks, to say the milk is the same thing as the curd, or the butter, or the ghee? No, says the king. But they came from it. Just so, says Nagasena: one state arises, another passes away, and the line runs on, neither the same nor another. Fourth, why a kitchen. Nobody stands over a pot of curd and argues about whether it is still the milk. They just know it came from the milk and wouldn't exist without it. The milk didn't hand over some hidden essence of milk. It changed, all the way through, and the curd is what that change became. So the baby in the photo isn't a stranger and isn't a frozen self either. It's milk, and the person looking at the photo is the butter. What carries on is the becoming itself, one form arising out of the last.
screen: `IF THE BABY WAS SOMEONE ELSE...` · `ONE THROUGH THE SAME BODY.` · `MILK, CURD, BUTTER, GHEE.` · `NO HIDDEN ESSENCE, ONLY CHANGE.` · then, large: `IT CAME FROM THE MILK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing changing form. Look around for something in the middle of becoming. Tea cooling. A plant leaning toward the window. Light shifting across the floor. Watch it for a moment. Then turn to your own hands resting in your lap. They were once small enough to grip one finger. Let them rest there, changed all the way through, and let the breath come and go. Nothing needs to be held still. The bell holds the time.
Milk to curd. Nagasena's kitchen picture: curd isn't the milk, and isn't something else; it came from the milk. Today's word.
Your line: milk to butter. Today, look at an old photo of yourself, or remember one, and name one thing in you now that came from that person. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

fork.reveal: the king says it isn't the milk, but it came from it. just so, says Nagasena: the line of a life runs on, neither the same nor another.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: curd. the second stage in Nagasena's milk image.

872.title: Why the good suffer
872.hook: the king asks why good people suffer; Nagasena answers carefully
872.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers point to this passage of the Questions of King Milinda to say that not all suffering is the result of past kamma, and that illness and accident have other causes too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, milk to curd: not the same, not another, but it came from the milk. Your line was milk to butter. What in you came from an earlier you? Today, the king's hardest question. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

The king has heard the mango and the milk. Deeds bear fruit; lives grow out of what was planted. So he takes the idea to its edge, where it hurts. The Buddha, he says, had cleared away every unwholesome deed. Then why, in the stories, did he ever suffer? Why did a splinter of rock wound his foot? Why was he ever sick? If every pain is the fruit of something done, the king says, then either the Buddha had bad deeds left, or the teaching is wrong. Pick one. It's a question heard in hospital waiting rooms too: why did this happen to someone who didn't deserve it?
screen: `DEEDS BEAR FRUIT. SO...` → `WHY DID THE BUDDHA SUFFER?` → `PICK ONE, SAYS THE KING.`

segments.voice: First, the careful answer. Nagasena won't pick either. He says the mistake is in the premise: not everything that is felt has kamma as its root. Second, the list. Pain, he says, can come from several causes. From the body's own workings, what the old medicine called wind, bile and phlegm. From the change of seasons. From careless treatment. From a sudden blow from outside. And from kamma. Kamma is one cause among them, not the only one. Those who say every pain is the result of past deeds, he says, go too far. Third, the Buddha's foot. The splinter of rock, Nagasena says, was not the ripening of some old deed. It came from someone else's act and from the plain fact of a stone breaking. The Buddha felt the pain. That did not mean he had earned it. Fourth, why this matters on an ordinary day. It's easy to hear the teaching on kamma as a verdict: you're sick, so you must have done something. Nagasena refuses that reading, in a book the tradition keeps. When someone is suffering, the question 'what did they do to deserve this?' may have no answer at all, because the suffering may not have come from anything they did. Bodies fail. Weather turns. Other people act. Stones fall. That leaves room for something besides judgment. It leaves room to sit beside the person, and to help. The king asked the hard question at full strength, and Nagasena answered without pretending it was easier than it was.
screen: `NOT EVERY PAIN HAS KAMMA AS ITS ROOT.` · `THE BODY, THE SEASONS, A BLOW, KAMMA.` · `THE BUDDHA'S FOOT: PAIN, NOT PAYMENT.` · `ROOM FOR HELP, NOT A VERDICT.` · then, large: `THE HARD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one unfair thing. Sit still for a moment. Bring to mind something that happened to someone, maybe you, that nobody deserved. You don't need to explain it, and you don't need to fix it in the next two minutes. Just let it be there, without reaching for a reason. If a judgment comes, they must have, I must have, notice it and set it down. Breathe beside it, the way you might sit beside a friend. The bell holds the time.
Why the good suffer. The king's question, and Nagasena's careful answer: kamma is one cause of pain among several, not the whole story. Today's word.
Your line: the hard question. Today, when you hear of someone's trouble, leave out 'they must have' and ask instead what would help. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

fork.reveal: he rejects the premise. pain can come from the body, the seasons, careless treatment, a blow from outside, or kamma: one cause among several.

what it means: Nagasena says not every pain has kamma as its root; the body, the seasons, careless treatment and accident cause pain too.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, Book 4 (the dilemma of the Buddha's pain: not all feeling has kamma as its root)

873.title: Like the ocean
873.hook: nibbana compared to the ocean, to a mountain peak, to space (Milinda, Book 4)
873.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often speak of nibbana by simile rather than definition, and Nagasena's comparisons to the ocean, a mountain peak and space are among those retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why the good suffer: kamma is one cause of pain among several, not a verdict. Your line was the hard question. Did you leave out a 'they must have'? Today, the king asks about the goal itself. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

Try describing the color blue to someone who has never seen color. Sooner or later the words turn into likenesses: cool like water, open like the sky. The king hits the same wall. He asks Nagasena about nibbana, the end of craving and suffering that the whole path points toward. Can you show me its shape, he asks, its size, its color, how long it lasts? No, says Nagasena. It can't be shown that way. Then is there nothing to say at all? There is, Nagasena answers. It can't be described by shape. But its qualities can be pointed to, one simile at a time.
screen: `DESCRIBE BLUE, WITHOUT SIGHT.` → `NIBBANA: SHAPE? SIZE? COLOR?` → `NO. BUT ITS QUALITIES, BY SIMILE.`

segments.voice: First, like the ocean. The ocean, Nagasena says, is vast and boundless, and all the rivers flowing into it never fill it up. Nibbana too is vast, and is not filled by all the beings who reach it. The ocean, he adds, does not keep a corpse; it washes it ashore. Nibbana too keeps none of the corpses of the defilements, greed and hatred and delusion. Second, like a mountain peak. A peak is lofty and cannot be shaken. It's hard to climb. Seeds don't take root on the bare summit. Nibbana, he says, is like that: high, unshakable, hard to reach, a place where the defilements can't grow, and free from liking and disliking, as a peak favors no one. Third, like space. Space is not born and does not grow old. It does not die and does not pass away. It can't be conquered and thieves can't carry it off. It rests on nothing, and it has no end. Birds move through it freely. Nibbana, Nagasena says, has those qualities. Fourth, why similes. Nagasena is not hiding something. He is being honest about what words can do. A shape would make nibbana one more thing in the world, something with edges, something to grab. A simile gives a direction instead: look toward the open sea, the high summit, the clear sky, and keep looking past them. The king asked for a description and got a set of windows. Each one shows a little, and none of them is the view itself. It's Nagasena's way of saying: this is real, and it's not an object.
screen: `OCEAN: VAST, NEVER FILLED.` · `PEAK: HIGH, UNSHAKABLE, HARD TO CLIMB.` · `SPACE: UNBORN, RESTING ON NOTHING.` · `A SET OF WINDOWS, NOT A SHAPE.` · then, large: `LIKE SPACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the sky. Go to a window, or step outside, or simply remember the sky from this morning. Let your eyes rest on the open part, not on clouds or buildings. Notice that it doesn't push back. It holds everything that moves through it and keeps none of it. Then close your eyes, if you like, and let that openness be the background for the breath. Thoughts move through like birds. The bell holds the time.
Like the ocean. Nagasena's way of pointing to nibbana: not by shape, but by simile, the ocean, the mountain peak and space. Today's word.
Your line: like space. Today, when something crowds your mind, look up once and let the open sky remind you that it can hold all of it. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

fork.reveal: he says it can't be shown by shape, then compares its qualities to the ocean, a mountain peak, and space.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, Book 4 (the similes for nibbana: the ocean, space, the mountain peak)

874.title: Kanishka's council
874.hook: the Kushan king's council in Kashmir, in the northern accounts
874.howItsDone: Northern Buddhist traditions, including Tibetan and Chinese histories, remember a council under King Kanishka, while the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka count their councils differently; each tradition keeps its own list.

segments.voice: Yesterday, like the ocean: Nagasena pointed to nibbana by simile, the ocean, the peak, and open space. Your line was like space. Did you look up? Today we leave the king's court and head north, to another king and another story. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

Sheets of copper, engraved line after line with commentary on the teaching, sealed inside a stupa so the words would last. That is the story the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang recorded about Kashmir. A few days ago we heard the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka remember a council under Ashoka, and a canon written on palm leaves. Travel north, into Kashmir and beyond, and the accounts kept there remember another gathering, under another king: Kanishka, a ruler of the Kushan empire.
screen: `COPPER SHEETS, SEALED IN A STUPA.` → `THE SOUTH REMEMBERS ITS COUNCILS.` → `THE NORTH REMEMBERS KANISHKA.`

segments.voice: First, the king. In the northern accounts, Kanishka is a powerful ruler who becomes a patron of the teaching. Tradition says he was troubled because the monks he consulted gave him different explanations of the same teachings, and he wanted to know which were sound. Second, the gathering. So, the accounts say, he called learned monks together in Kashmir. Some accounts name a monk called Vasumitra as the one who led it, and some link the poet Ashvaghosha with it too. Others place the meeting somewhere else. The stories agree on the king and the purpose more than on the details. Third, the work. The monks did not write a new canon, in these accounts. They wrote commentaries: long explanations of the teaching and of the finer points of the Abhidharma, the systematic analysis of mind and experience. That's where the copper sheets come in: Xuanzang recorded a tradition that these commentaries were engraved on them and sealed inside a stupa. Fourth, why it matters that the accounts differ. The Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka don't include this council in their list. The northern schools, and the Tibetan and Chinese histories that drew on them, remember it. Nobody has to decide here which list is right. What's worth noticing is that Buddhism was already more than one living tradition, with more than one memory of its own past. Each community kept the councils that shaped its own texts. Hearing the northern account doesn't cancel the southern one. It's another community, telling the story the way it was told to them.
screen: `A KING TROUBLED BY MANY EXPLANATIONS.` · `LEARNED MONKS GATHER IN KASHMIR.` · `COMMENTARIES, SAID TO BE SEALED IN A STUPA.` · `NORTH AND SOUTH REMEMBER DIFFERENT COUNCILS.` · then, large: `THE NORTHERN ACCOUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how a story changes with the place that tells it. Let the body be still for a moment. Bring to mind something that is told or done one way where you grew up and another way somewhere else: a holiday, a recipe, a saint's story, the name for a meal. Let both versions sit side by side, without choosing a winner. Notice what each place keeps and what each one leaves out. Then let both rest, and come back to the breath, which needs no version at all. The bell holds the time.
Kanishka's council. The gathering of monks in Kashmir under the Kushan king, remembered in the northern accounts, where commentaries on the teaching were composed. Today's word.
Your line: the northern account. Today, when you hear a story told differently from the way you know it, ask who kept that version, and why. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

screen: `DAY 874 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A NEW WAVE OF SUTRAS.`

875.title: A new wave of sutras
875.hook: new scriptures appear, centered on the bodhisattva who waits to free all beings
875.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities, sutras such as the Heart Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Lotus Sutra are chanted and studied, and the bodhisattva vow, to seek awakening for the sake of all beings, is taken in ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the northern account: Kanishka's council, remembered in the north and not in the south. This week Nagasena lit a flame from a flame, judged a stolen mango, turned milk to curd, took on the hard question, and pointed at space. Then the north told its own story. Today, a new kind of sutra. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

A sutra opens the way the old ones do: thus have I heard. The Buddha is seated among his followers. But the crowd is different. Alongside the monks sit beings called bodhisattvas, whole assemblies of them, and the teaching that follows sounds new. In India, texts like this began to circulate: the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, the Lotus Sutra, and others. The communities that treasured them gave their way a name. Mahayana. The great vehicle.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `A CROWD OF BODHISATTVAS.` → `MAHAYANA: THE GREAT VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: First, the figure at the center. A bodhisattva is a being set on full awakening. The word isn't new: we met the bodhisatta in the Jataka tales, the Buddha in his earlier lives, and the Theravada tradition honors that path too. What the new sutras do is hold it up as a path for many to walk, not only the one who became the Buddha. Second, the vow. In these texts the bodhisattva sets out to awaken not for themselves alone but for the sake of all beings. One popular way of putting it is that the bodhisattva waits at the threshold of nibbana until every being can pass through. Some Mahayana teachers put it differently: not waiting, but working, life after life, until all are free. Either way, the heart of it is the same three words. For all beings. Third, a twist. The Diamond Sutra, one of the Perfection of Wisdom texts, has the Buddha say that a bodhisattva should resolve to lead all beings to nibbana, and yet hold that no being at all has been led there. If the bodhisattva thinks of a self, a being, a person, he is no bodhisattva. It echoes Nagasena's chariot, turned toward compassion: help everyone, and don't build a self out of the helping. Fourth, where the texts came from. Followers of these sutras received them as the Buddha's word. A story some tell says certain texts were kept by the nagas, serpent beings, until the right teacher came for them. Historians say simply that these texts appear later than the older collections. Both views are held. Our next days follow the places where these texts were studied.
screen: `THE BODHISATTVA: SET ON AWAKENING.` · `THE VOW: FOR THE SAKE OF ALL BEINGS.` · `HELP ALL, AND BUILD NO SELF FROM IT.` · `RECEIVED AS THE BUDDHA'S WORD.` · then, large: `FOR ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone who waits for others. The friend who walks at the slow one's pace. The parent who eats last. The coworker who stays until everyone's file is in. Bring one face to mind and stay with it. Notice what their waiting gives. Then, gently, widen it: the people around them, the people around those. Let the circle grow as far as it will. Breathe in it. The bell holds the time.
Mahayana. The great vehicle: the name taken by communities following the new sutras, with the bodhisattva and the vow for all beings at their center. Today's word.
Your line: for all beings. Today, slow down once for someone who's behind you, on the stairs, in a line, in a conversation, and let them catch up. Day eight hundred seventy-five.
